claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.

A GeoDeploy deployment request consists of target geos (traffic share and data-residency rule of EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape, and constraints (allowed providers, provider count, budget).

In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app does all math and never makes judgment calls; Jev never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS and decides nothing.
GeoDeploy uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure when enumerating candidate regions.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost per candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy won't provision unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives: choice(), score(), and noul().
Jev's choice() picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() rates something against a rubric; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, a hallucinated region or made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates.

In a single call GeoDeploy asks Jev for one selection, five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard noul checks (residency, capacity), and a fallback choice.
The question code lives in packages/decide/src/questions.ts in the GeoDeploy repo.
The TypeSafe SDK package is @typesafe-ai/sdk and exports choice, noul, and score.
TypeSafe's advice for rubrics is to "describe situations, not degrees."
The TypeSafeClient exposes a systemOne method taking state and questions, returning answers with fields such as selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, coverage.score.
GeoDeploy ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because weights live in code, GeoDeploy can re-tune the ranking without calling Jev again.
The GeoDeploy weight profiles have specific values, e.g. latency-optimized: cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12.
In GeoDeploy's composite score, sprawl risk is subtracted.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow from the provider (AWS means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); new-cluster region 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human); region with existing stack 0.75 (keep existing); ingress/autoscaling module 0.85 (registry default); node-pool sizing 0.60 (bin-packing result); global floor 0.50 (drop AI path for that geo).
The residency check is in packages/decide/src/engine.ts in the GeoDeploy repo.
Each AiPathAborted carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic path comparing prices across providers while enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

With self-driving mode enabled via `geodeploy monitor`, the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.

In self-driving mode, code rather than Jev computes node-count changes; above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically, between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval, and below 0.70 GeoDeploy falls back to a deterministic per-region rule.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median request latency or error rates.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
